questions.stem: What is a force?
options: The energy stored in an object
A push or a pull on an object
questions.explanation: Forces are pushes and pulls. Speed, mass and energy are different quantities.
questions.teaching:
Forces are the starting point of mechanics, and the definition is deliberately broad.

Anything that pushes or pulls counts, whether or not anything moves — you can push a wall without shifting it. Forces have both size and direction, which is why they are drawn as arrows, and they always act between two objects rather than belonging to one. They are measured in newtons. What forces do is change motion: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or change its direction. If nothing about the motion changes, the forces present are balanced.

questions.stem: What unit is force measured in?
questions.explanation: Force is in newtons. Kilograms measure mass and joules measure energy.
questions.teaching:
Several physical quantities are named after scientists, and mixing up which unit belongs to which quantity is the usual error here.

A force is a push or a pull, and its unit is named after Isaac Newton — defined as the force needed to accelerate one kilogram by one metre per second every second. Roughly speaking, holding a small apple takes about one of them. Energy is measured in joules, power in watts, and pressure in pascals. Weight is a force, so it belongs in the first unit, while mass is in kilograms and is not a force at all.

questions.stem: What happens when the forces on an object are balanced?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces mean no change in motion — a stationary object stays still and a moving one continues at constant speed.

questions.stem: What happens when forces on an object are unbalanced?
options: Its motion changes — it speeds up, slows down or changes direction
It moves at a steady speed in the direction of the larger force
questions.explanation: Unbalanced forces cause acceleration in the direction of the larger force.

questions.stem: What is friction?
options: A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact
A force that pulls objects towards Earth
A force that pushes objects up in water
The energy of a moving object
questions.explanation: Friction always acts against the direction of movement.
questions.teaching:
Friction is what makes everyday motion misleading. It stops the book you slide across a table, which makes it look as though motion needs constant pushing — but friction is a force acting, not an absence of one.

It arises wherever surfaces are in contact, and it always acts against the direction of sliding. Air resistance is the same idea for an object moving through a fluid. It is not gravity: gravity pulls downwards regardless of whether anything is sliding, and both act at once on a box you are pushing across a floor. Friction is also useful — without it you could not walk, and brakes would not work.

questions.stem: What is gravity?
options: The same thing as weight in kilograms
A force that pushes objects apart
A force of attraction between objects with mass
A force that only acts on falling objects
questions.explanation: Gravity is attraction due to mass. Weight is the force gravity exerts on a particular mass.

questions.stem: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Weight is measured in kilograms and mass in newtons
Mass changes on the Moon but weight does not
Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on that mass
questions.explanation: Mass stays the same everywhere; weight changes with gravitational strength — you would weigh less on the Moon but have the same mass.

questions.stem: What unit is energy measured in?
questions.explanation: Energy is in joules. Watts measure power, which is energy per second.
questions.teaching:
Energy and force are different quantities with different units, and so is power, so it is worth sorting all three.

Force is a push or pull, measured in units named after Newton. Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in units named after James Joule — and the same unit covers every form, whether kinetic, chemical or thermal, which is what makes energy transfers comparable. Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts, where one watt is one unit of energy per second. Match the quantity to the scientist and these questions become quick.

questions.stem: What is kinetic energy?
options: The energy stored in an object's position
The energy stored in chemical bonds
Energy that has been lost as heat
The energy an object has because it is moving
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed. Stored energy due to position is gravitational potential energy.

questions.stem: What is gravitational potential energy?
options: Energy stored because of an object's height above the ground
Energy an object has because it is moving
Energy stored in a stretched spring
questions.explanation: Lifting something stores energy that is released if it falls. A stretched spring stores elastic potential energy instead.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple machine?
questions.explanation: The six simple machines are the lever, inclined plane, wedge, pulley, screw, and wheel and axle.
questions.teaching:
Simple machines change the size or direction of a force, letting a small effort move a large load — they do not create energy.

There are six classic types: the lever, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, the pulley and the wheel and axle. A crowbar, a ramp, an axe, a flight of stairs and a tap all use one or more. Complex machines are combinations of them. The trade-off is always the same: what you gain in force you lose in distance, because the work done cannot exceed the work put in.

questions.stem: What does a simple machine do to a force?
options: Changes its size or direction to make a task easier
questions.explanation: Machines redirect or multiply force. They never create energy.

questions.stem: What is an inclined plane used for?
options: Raising a load using a smaller force over a longer distance
questions.explanation: A ramp trades a smaller force for a longer distance — the total work is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is a screw most like?
options: A wedge with two flat sides
An inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder
A lever with a fixed pivot
questions.explanation: The thread is a spiral ramp, which is why turning a screw drives it forward with great force.

questions.stem: What does a pulley do?
options: Changes the direction of a force, and with several pulleys reduces the force needed
Removes the weight of the load
questions.explanation: A single pulley redirects; a system of pulleys reduces the force needed at the cost of pulling more rope.

questions.stem: What is a lever's pivot point called?
questions.explanation: A lever has effort, load and fulcrum. Where the fulcrum sits determines the advantage.
questions.teaching:
A lever has three parts, and identifying them is what lets you predict how it will behave.

The effort is the force you apply. The load is the force you are trying to overcome. And between or beyond them is the fixed point the bar turns about. Where that fixed point sits relative to the other two determines the class of lever: between them in a seesaw or crowbar, with the load between in a wheelbarrow, with the effort between in tweezers or your forearm. The further the effort is from the turning point, the less force you need.

questions.stem: Which form of energy is stored in food and fuels?
questions.explanation: Chemical energy is stored in bonds and released in reactions such as respiration or combustion.
questions.teaching:
Energy is classified into stores, and naming the right one means asking where the energy is being held.

Movement gives kinetic. Height in a gravitational field gives gravitational potential. Stretching or squashing gives elastic potential. And energy held in the bonds between atoms, released when those bonds are rearranged in a reaction, is a store of its own — it is what makes petrol, batteries and a bowl of pasta all useful. Digestion and combustion both release it, which is why food and fuel belong to the same category despite feeling very different.

questions.stem: What is thermal energy?
options: Energy associated with the temperature of an object
Energy stored in a stretched spring
The energy of a moving object only
questions.explanation: Thermal energy relates to the movement of particles within a substance.

questions.stem: What is an energy transformation?
options: Energy moving from one place to another
Energy changing from one form to another
questions.explanation: Transformation changes the form; transfer moves it. Neither creates or destroys energy.

questions.stem: What is an energy audit of a home?
options: A calculation of a home's value
A survey of where and how much energy is used
A measurement of how much a house weighs
A test of a home's electrical safety only
questions.explanation: An audit identifies where energy goes so it can be reduced — the practical application in the curriculum.

questions.stem: A car travels at a constant speed in a straight line. What can you say about the forces?
options: Only the driving force acts, with no resistance opposing it
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means balanced forces. Forces are certainly present — the engine's drive and friction cancel out.

questions.stem: Why does a ball rolling on grass stop sooner than on a smooth floor?
options: Grass produces more friction, which is an unbalanced force opposing motion
The ball loses mass on grass
The ball has no energy on grass
questions.explanation: Greater friction means a larger opposing force, so the ball decelerates faster.

questions.stem: A 10 kg box is pushed with 30 N while friction resists with 30 N. What happens?
options: It continues at constant speed or stays still
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite forces are balanced, so there is no change in motion.

questions.stem: Why does a ramp make it easier to lift a heavy load?
options: The same work is done with a smaller force over a longer distance
The ramp reduces the load's mass
The ramp adds energy to the load
questions.explanation: Machines trade force for distance. The energy required is the same, or slightly more once friction is included.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown upwards. Describe the energy change as it rises.
options: Kinetic energy is transformed into gravitational potential energy
Energy is destroyed as it slows
questions.explanation: It slows as it climbs, losing kinetic energy and gaining potential energy. On the way down the exchange reverses.

questions.stem: Which statement about energy in a torch is correct?
options: Chemical energy in the battery becomes electrical, then light and thermal energy
Light energy is created from nothing
Only light energy is produced, with no waste
questions.explanation: Every transformation produces some waste thermal energy. A torch is never 100 per cent efficient.

questions.stem: Why is no machine 100 per cent efficient?
options: Energy leaks out of the universe
Some energy is always transferred to the surroundings, usually as heat
questions.explanation: Friction and other losses always divert some energy. Energy is conserved, but not all of it ends up doing the useful job.

questions.stem: Two identical balls are dropped from different heights. Which has more kinetic energy on landing?
options: They land with equal kinetic energy
The one dropped from higher up
The one dropped from lower down
questions.explanation: More height means more stored gravitational potential energy to convert into kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Why does a heavier object need a larger force to accelerate at the same rate?
options: Heavier objects are pulled less by gravity
Heavier objects need more force only when moving uphill
Greater mass resists a change in motion more
questions.explanation: Mass is a measure of resistance to change in motion, which is why the same push produces less acceleration on a heavier object.

questions.stem: A force diagram shows a 50 N downward arrow and a 50 N upward arrow on a book. What does this show?
options: The book's weight is balanced by the table pushing up
The book is about to lift up
questions.explanation: The table exerts an upward normal force equal to the weight, so the forces are balanced and the book stays still.

questions.stem: How could a household reduce energy use based on an audit?
options: Replace the largest energy users, such as inefficient heating, with more efficient options
Switch off the smallest appliances only
questions.explanation: Audits direct effort to where the energy actually goes. Heating and cooling usually dominate, so small devices matter less.

questions.stem: Why is a wedge described as a simple machine?
options: It converts a downward force into sideways forces that split material
questions.explanation: An axe head is a moving inclined plane, redirecting force sideways.

questions.stem: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity. Explain in terms of forces.
options: Air resistance has become greater than weight
Air resistance has grown until it balances weight, so there is no further acceleration
Weight has decreased during the fall
questions.explanation: Air resistance rises with speed until it equals weight. The forces are then balanced and speed becomes constant — not zero.

questions.stem: Why does a longer spanner make it easier to loosen a tight bolt?
options: A force applied further from the pivot has a greater turning effect
A longer spanner reduces friction in the bolt
questions.explanation: Turning effect depends on force multiplied by distance from the pivot, so the same effort further out does more.

questions.stem: A pulley system lets a person lift 200 N using 50 N of effort. What is the trade-off?
options: They must pull about four times as much rope
Energy is created by the pulleys
questions.explanation: Work in equals work out (ignoring friction), so reducing force by four means increasing distance by four.

questions.stem: Which observation best demonstrates that energy is conserved rather than destroyed?
options: A ball bouncing lower each time, with the missing energy detectable as heat and sound
A ball rolling along a level floor at a steady speed for as long as the surface stays smooth
A battery running a torch until it goes flat, after which no further energy can be drawn from it
A pendulum swinging back to almost the same height on the far side of every single swing
questions.explanation: Accounting for where the 'lost' energy went is what demonstrates conservation. Simply observing something stop does not.

questions.stem: A student says 'the machine reduces the work needed'. What is the accurate statement?
options: It reduces the force needed, but the work is the same or slightly greater
It reduces both force and work
It reduces the energy needed to zero
questions.explanation: Work is force times distance. Machines redistribute the two; friction means total work usually rises slightly.

questions.stem: Why does a small mass at high speed sometimes carry more kinetic energy than a large mass moving slowly?
options: Kinetic energy depends on mass alone, so the heavier object must win
Kinetic energy rises with the square of speed but only in proportion to mass
Kinetic energy rises in proportion to speed, not to its square
A small mass loses energy to friction more slowly than a large one
questions.explanation: Because speed is squared, a modest increase in speed outweighs a large increase in mass — this is the physics behind speed limits.

questions.stem: A see-saw balances with a heavy child close to the pivot and a lighter child far from it. Explain.
options: The pivot shifts towards the heavier child until it balances
The two children must have nearly equal mass
Turning effect depends on both force and distance from the pivot, and the two products are equal
Weight acts downwards, so only the two masses decide the balance
questions.explanation: Force multiplied by distance is what balances, not weight alone. This is the lever principle in action.

questions.stem: What is speed?
options: How far something travels in a given time
The force acting on an object
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time. Velocity adds a direction.

questions.stem: What is acceleration?
options: A change in an object's speed or direction
Constant motion in a straight line
questions.explanation: Slowing down and turning are both accelerations, not just speeding up.

questions.stem: What is air resistance?
options: A force that speeds objects up
A friction force from air opposing motion through it
questions.explanation: Air resistance grows with speed, which is why falling objects reach a terminal velocity.

questions.stem: What is upthrust?
options: An upward force from a fluid on an object in it
questions.explanation: Upthrust is why objects feel lighter in water and why things float.

questions.stem: What is elastic potential energy?
options: Energy stored in a stretched or squashed object
questions.explanation: A stretched rubber band or compressed spring stores elastic potential energy.

questions.stem: What is sound energy?
options: Energy carried by vibrations through a material
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium, which is why it cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.stem: What is the law of conservation of energy?
options: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed
questions.explanation: Energy that appears lost has usually been transferred to the surroundings as heat.

questions.stem: What is work in physics?
options: The energy stored in an object
Force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force
questions.explanation: If nothing moves, no work is done in the physics sense, however hard you push.

questions.stem: What is power?
options: The rate at which energy is transferred
questions.explanation: Power is energy per second, measured in watts.
questions.teaching:
Energy and power sound interchangeable in everyday speech and are quite different in physics.

Energy is an amount, like litres in a tank. Power is how fast that amount is transferred or used, like litres per second — so it is a rate, and its unit is defined as one joule per second. A 2000-watt kettle and a 1000-watt one can deliver exactly the same energy if the slower one runs twice as long. That distinction is why electricity bills are in kilowatt-hours: a rate multiplied by a time, which gives an amount.

questions.stem: Why does a parachute slow a falling skydiver?
options: It adds upward thrust from an engine
It greatly increases air resistance, unbalancing the forces against motion
questions.explanation: The larger surface area increases drag until it exceeds weight, slowing the descent to a new, lower terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A book rests on a table. Name the two main balanced forces.
options: Weight downwards and the table's normal force upwards
questions.explanation: The table pushes up with a force equal to the book's weight.

questions.stem: Why is it harder to push a heavy box on carpet than on polished floor?
options: The box gains mass on carpet
questions.explanation: Rougher surfaces increase the friction force opposing motion.

questions.stem: A cyclist stops pedalling and gradually slows. Which forces act?
options: Friction and air resistance oppose the motion
questions.explanation: Without a driving force, the resistive forces are unbalanced and produce deceleration.

questions.stem: How is energy transformed in a hydroelectric power station?
options: Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic, then electrical energy
questions.explanation: Falling water drives turbines that drive generators.

questions.stem: Why do bicycles have gears?
options: Gears change the force and distance trade-off to suit the terrain
questions.explanation: Low gears trade distance for force on hills; high gears do the reverse on flat ground.

questions.stem: Which change would double a lever's turning effect with the same force?
options: Applying the force twice as far from the pivot
Applying the force closer to the pivot
questions.explanation: Turning effect is force times distance from the pivot.

questions.stem: Why does a heavier vehicle need a longer distance to stop?
options: More mass means more kinetic energy to remove at the same braking force
Heavier vehicles have more air resistance slowing them
Heavier vehicles carry their weight further from the wheels
Heavier vehicles need more force before the brakes grip
questions.explanation: The brakes must dissipate more energy, so the vehicle travels further while doing so.

questions.stem: How does a ramp illustrate that machines do not create energy?
options: The reduced force is offset by the greater distance travelled
The ramp adds energy to the load
questions.explanation: Work in equals work out, ignoring friction — the trade is force for distance.

questions.stem: Two objects of different mass are dropped in a vacuum. What happens?
options: They fall at the same rate
questions.explanation: Without air resistance, acceleration due to gravity is the same for all masses — famously demonstrated on the Moon.

questions.stem: Why is a crumple zone in a car a safety feature?
options: It extends the time of the collision, reducing the forces on occupants
questions.explanation: Spreading the same change in motion over a longer time reduces the peak force.

questions.stem: A student says energy is 'used up' by a light bulb. What is the accurate description?
options: It is transformed into light and thermal energy that spread into the surroundings
It is stored in the bulb until the light is switched off
It is converted entirely into light with no waste
It is carried away by the current and returned to the supply
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved. What changes is its form and how useful it remains.

questions.stem: Why does a bouncing ball never return to its original height?
options: Some energy is transferred to heat and sound at each bounce
Air resistance removes energy only while the ball is rising
The ball compresses slightly less on each bounce
Gravitational energy is not fully recovered at the top
questions.explanation: Tracking where the energy goes demonstrates conservation rather than contradicting it.

questions.stem: Why does pushing a door near the hinges require more force than at the handle?
options: The turning effect depends on distance from the pivot, which is small near the hinges
The door is heavier near the hinges
Friction is greater at the hinges
questions.explanation: This is why handles are fitted as far from the hinge as possible.

questions.stem: What is weight?
options: The force of gravity acting on a mass
The amount of matter in an object
questions.explanation: Weight is a force measured in newtons; mass is in kilograms.
questions.teaching:
In ordinary speech the two words are interchangeable. In physics they are different quantities with different units, and exam questions are frequently built on exactly that gap.

One of them measures how much matter something contains. It is identical on Earth, on the Moon and drifting in deep space, and it is recorded in kilograms. The other is a pull — what a gravitational field does to that matter — and it is recorded in newtons, like every other force. Take an astronaut to the Moon, where the field is about a sixth of Earth's, and the first quantity is unchanged while the second drops to a sixth. A bathroom scale actually senses the pull and then converts, assuming you are standing on Earth.

questions.stem: What is a contact force?
options: A force acting at a distance
A force that acts through a field rather than by touching
A force that only acts on objects at rest
A force acting only when two objects touch
questions.explanation: Friction and normal force are contact forces; gravity and magnetism act at a distance.

questions.stem: What is a non-contact force?
options: A force that acts without objects touching
questions.explanation: Gravity, magnetism and electrostatic force all act at a distance.

questions.stem: What is thrust?
options: A driving force pushing an object forward
questions.explanation: An engine or rocket provides thrust against drag.
questions.teaching:
Forces acting on a moving vehicle or aircraft have standard names, and the four are worth learning as a set.

Weight pulls it downwards. Lift, on an aircraft, acts upwards. Drag opposes motion through air or water. And the force generated to push it forwards — by an engine, a propeller, a jet, or a rocket — completes the set. In steady flight, opposite pairs balance. Speeding up means the forward force exceeds drag; slowing down means the reverse. Naming which force is which is the first step in almost every force diagram question.

questions.stem: What is drag?
options: A resistive force from a fluid opposing motion
questions.explanation: Air resistance and water resistance are both drag forces.

questions.stem: What is a force diagram?
options: A drawing using arrows to show the forces on an object
A graph of speed over time
questions.explanation: Arrow length shows size and arrow direction shows the force's direction.

questions.stem: What does the length of an arrow in a force diagram represent?
questions.explanation: Longer arrows represent larger forces.

questions.stem: What is chemical potential energy?
options: Energy stored in the bonds of a substance
questions.explanation: Food, fuel and batteries all store chemical energy.

questions.stem: Which energy transformation happens in a solar panel?
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electricity.

questions.stem: What is efficiency?
options: The proportion of input energy that becomes useful output
questions.explanation: The remainder is transferred to the surroundings, usually as heat.

questions.stem: Two forces of 8 N and 5 N act in opposite directions. What is the resultant?
options: 3 N in the direction of the 8 N force
3 N in the direction of the 5 N force
questions.explanation: Opposing forces subtract, and the resultant acts in the direction of the larger.

questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 4 N act in the same direction. What is the resultant?
questions.explanation: Forces acting the same way add together, giving 10 N. They only subtract when they act in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A lift moves upwards at constant speed. What can you say about the forces?
questions.explanation: Constant velocity always means balanced forces, even when moving.

questions.stem: Why is a rough surface used on the soles of sports shoes?
options: To increase friction and improve grip
questions.explanation: Grip depends on friction between shoe and ground.

questions.stem: A pendulum swings. Describe the energy changes at the highest point.
options: Energy is destroyed at the top
Energy is entirely gravitational potential, with no kinetic energy
questions.explanation: At the extremes the pendulum is momentarily stationary, so all its energy is potential.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is a ramp used to load a truck?
questions.explanation: A ramp reduces the force needed by increasing the distance travelled.

questions.stem: Why is an energy audit useful for a household?
options: It identifies the biggest energy users so effort targets the largest savings
It reduces the cost of electricity directly
questions.explanation: Prioritising by size of use is the practical value of an audit.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object and a 10 kg object are pushed with equal force on a frictionless surface. Compare their acceleration.
options: The 2 kg object accelerates five times as much
questions.explanation: For the same force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

questions.stem: Why does a seatbelt reduce injury in a crash?
options: It increases the force on the body but spreads that force over a much wider area of contact
It holds the passenger completely still so that the car and the body stop at the same instant
It removes the passenger's momentum entirely before the car itself begins to slow down
It applies the stopping force over a longer time and spreads it across stronger parts of the body
questions.explanation: Extending the time of the change in motion reduces the peak force experienced.

questions.stem: Why is energy described as conserved even though machines waste it?
options: Conservation applies only to perfect machines
Wasted energy is transferred to the surroundings, not destroyed
questions.explanation: Efficiency is about how much becomes useful, not about how much exists.

questions.stem: Which statement about a machine's mechanical advantage is correct?
options: It describes how much the output force exceeds the input force
It is always greater than the efficiency
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage is a force ratio and is always paid for in distance.

questions.stem: Which measurement would show that a light bulb is inefficient?
options: Measuring the current it draws and comparing that with a bulb of equal brightness
Comparing electrical energy supplied with light energy emitted and finding a large difference
Recording how long the bulb takes to reach full brightness after switching on
Checking whether it dims when other appliances share the same circuit
questions.explanation: Efficiency needs both input and useful output; the difference usually appears as heat.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 30 km in 5 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 30 / 5 = 6 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 150, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 120 km in 6 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 120 / 6 = 20 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 720, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 25 km in 5 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 25 / 5 = 5 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 125, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 60 km in 6 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 60 / 6 = 10 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 360, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 30 km in 6 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 30 / 6 = 5 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 180, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 16 km in 2 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 16 / 2 = 8 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 32, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 72 km in 6 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 72 / 6 = 12 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 432, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 8 km in 2 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 8 / 2 = 4 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 16, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 24 km in 4 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 24 / 4 = 6 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 96, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 24 km in 3 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 24 / 3 = 8 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 72, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 100 km in 5 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 100 / 5 = 20 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 500, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 80 km in 4 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 80 / 4 = 20 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 320, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 36 km in 6 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 36 / 6 = 6 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 216, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 10 km in 2 hours. What is their average speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 10 / 2 = 5 km/h. The unit tells you the operation — 'km per hour' means kilometres for each single hour, so you are sharing the distance across the hours. Multiplying instead gives 20, which has units of km-hours and describes nothing physical.
